rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the Prophet moved his tongue with revelation to memorize it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan sahih.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The Muslim and Bukhari account says the Prophet listened to Gabriel recite, then recited as taught; Ibn Abbas and Saʿid demonstrate the lip movement.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جبير عن ابن عباس قال: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يعالج من التنزيل شدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gathers the revelation in the Prophet’s breast and recites it to him; he is to listen and follow its recitation.
rows.anchor: قال جمعه في صدرك ثم تقرؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi compares this prohibition with the command not to hasten the Qur’an before its revelation is complete.
rows.anchor: ولا تعجل بالقرآن من قبل إن يقضى إليك وحيه

rows.speaker: عامر الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi says the Prophet hurried from love of the revelation and sweetness on his tongue; he was told to wait so its connected parts could come together.
rows.anchor: قال عامر الشعبي: إنما كان يعجل بذكره إذا نزل عليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet moved his tongue from fear of forgetting; this occasion is linked to commands about waiting and preservation.
rows.anchor: لا تحرك به لسانك } " قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ treats qirāʾa and Qurʾān as verbal nouns; Qurʾānah here means recitation to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والقراءة والقرآن في قول الفراء مصدران

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada interprets following the recitation as following the Qur’an’s laws and rulings.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: «فاتبع قرآنه» أي فاتبع شرائعه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says God will explain the Qur’an’s legal limits and lawful and forbidden matters.
rows.anchor: أي تفسير ما فيه من الحدود والحلال والحرام قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the explanation as clarifying the Qur’an’s promises and threats and bringing them to pass.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ثم إن علينا بيان ما فيه من الوعد والوعيد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says God will make the Qur’an clear through the Prophet’s tongue.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي إن علينا أن نبينه بلسانك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas takes kalla to say Abu Jahl will not believe in the Qur’an’s interpretation and clarification.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أي إن أبا جهل لا يؤمن بتفسير القرآن

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation addresses Meccan unbelievers: they do not pray or purify themselves.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي «كلا» لا يصلون ولا يزكون يريد كفار مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi identifies the addressees as Meccan unbelievers, al-ʿājila as this world and its life, and leaving the hereafter as abandoning its deeds.
rows.anchor: أي الدار الدنيا والحياة فيها

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some exegesis identifies the hereafter here specifically as Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض التفسير قال: الآخرة الجنة

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Medinese and Kufan readers use second-person forms; Abu Ubayd selects this direct address despite the alternative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أهل المدينة والكوفيون «بل تحبون» «وتذرون» بالتاء فيهما على الخطاب واختاره أبو عبيد

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Other readers use third-person forms; Abu Hatim prefers them as a return to al-insān, understood collectively as people.
rows.anchor: الباقون بالياء على الخبر، وهو اختيار أبي حاتم، فمن قرأ بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second-person reading confronts the unbelievers with blame, making the point more forceful.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالتاء فعلى أنه واجههم بالتقريع لأن ذلك أبلغ في المقصود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi supports this description of people loving the immediate life and leaving the hereafter with a parallel in Sūrat al-Insān.
rows.anchor: إن هؤلاء يحبون العاجلة ويذرون ورآءهم يوما ثقيلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed poem depicts an unparalleled separation after hope of reunion has ended.
rows.anchor: فراق ليس يشبهه فراق قد انقطع الرجاء عن التلاق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and others say the last hardship of this world joins the first hardship of the next.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عباس والحسن وغيرهما

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi and others understand legs twisting together from the agony of death.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي وغيره: المعنى التفت ساقا الإنسان عند الموت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada points to a dying person striking one leg against the other.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: أما رأيته إذا أشرف على الموت يضرب إحدى رجليه

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib and al-Hasan say the legs are folded together in the shroud.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن المسيب والحسن أيضا: هما ساقا الإنسان إذا التفتا في الكفن

rows.speaker: زيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Aslam understands the shroud’s leg as wrapping against the dead person’s leg.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن أسلم: التفت ساق الكفن بساق الميت

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan also says the legs die and the shins stiffen so they no longer carry the person.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن أيضا: ماتت رجلاه ويبست ساقاه فلم تحملاه

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas prefers the view that death’s final worldly hardship meets the first hardship of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: قال النحاس: القول الأول أحسنها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ali ibn Abi Talha transmits Ibn Abbas’s view that the last worldly day meets the first hereafter day, unless God has mercy, as death’s agony meets the encounter’s terror.
rows.anchor: وروى علي بن أبي طلحة عن ابن عباس: { والتفت الساق بالساق } قال: آخر يوم من الدنيا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses the phrase as affliction upon affliction, with hardships following one another.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: ببلاء ببلاء. يقول: تتابعت عليه الشدائد

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd say people prepare the body while angels prepare the soul, two severe matters at once.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك وابن زيد: اجتمع عليه أمران شديدان: الناس يجهزون جسده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabs use ساق for great trials, as in idioms that the world or war stands upon a ساق and a cited war poem.
rows.anchor: والعرب لا تذكر الساق إلا في المحن والشدائد العظام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the disbeliever’s soul is punished as it leaves the body, then comes the resurrection’s hardship.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: الكافر تعذب روحه عند خروج نفسه، فهذه الساق الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi glosses the destination as your Creator, that day as the Resurrection, and al-masāq as the return.
rows.anchor: أي إلى خالقك { يومئذ } أي يوم القيامة { المساق } أي المرجع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A tafsir says the person is driven to God by the angel who recorded his evil deeds.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض التفاسير قال: يسوقه ملكه الذي كان يحفظ عليه السيئات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-masāq is the verbal noun of sāqa yasūqu, like al-maqāl from qāla yaqūlu.
rows.anchor: والمساق: المصدر من ساق يسوق، كالمقال من قال يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi’s preferred view, attributed to Ibn Abbas, is that Abu Jahl neither believed nor prayed.
rows.anchor: أي لم يصدق أبو جهل ولم يصل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view returns the generic human to al-insān at the sūra’s beginning.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يرجع هذا إلى الإنسان في أول السورة، وهو اسم جنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial concerns the message; the prayer clause is glossed as supplicating to God and praying for His Messenger.
rows.anchor: أي لم يصدق بالرسالة «ولا صلى» ودعا لربه، وصلى على رسوله

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says he did not believe God’s Book and did not pray to God.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: فلا صدق بكتاب الله، ولا صلى لله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes denial as failure to give wealth stored with God and prayer as neglect of prescribed prayers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ولا صدق بمال له، ذخرا له عند الله، ولا صلى الصلوات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view reads the paired failures as lack of faith in the heart and lack of bodily action.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فلا آمن بقلبه ولا عمل ببدنه

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says lā can mean lam for past negation and is commonly paired with another lā.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: «لا» بمعنى لم ولكنه يقرن بغيره تقول العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi distinguishes 90:11: there lā means afalā, why did he not, with the interrogative alif omitted.
rows.anchor: ليس من هذا القبيل لأن معناه أفلا اقتحم أي فهلا اقتحم، فحذف ألف الاستفهام

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash reads lā as past negation, as with 90:11; no paired negative is required, and lā dhahaba means he did not go.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: { فلا صدق } أي لم يصدق كقوله: { فلا اقتحم } أي لم يقتحم

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr’s line is cited as evidence that lā can negate a past verb.
rows.anchor: قول زهير: فلا هو أبداها ولم يتقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man denied the Qur’an and turned away from faith.
rows.anchor: أي كذب بالقرآن وتولى عن الإيمان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and others call the return home an arrogant strut; Mujahid identifies the man as Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: قاله مجاهد وغيره. مجاهد: المراد به أبو جهل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation derives yamatta from al-matā, the back, and means twisting the back.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «يتمطى» من المطا وهو الظهر، والمعنى يلوي مطاه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another derives it from yatomattaṭ, lazy or heavy stretching; ṭāʾ became yāʾ to avoid doubling, conveying disregard and arrogance.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أصله يتمطط، وهو التمدد من التكسل والتثاقل، فهو يتثاقل عن الداعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi explains the strut as stretching and twisting the back; al-muṭīṭa is thick water at a basin’s bottom because it stretches.
rows.anchor: والتمطي يدل على قلة الاكتراث، وهو التمدد، كأنه يمد ظهره ويلويه من التبختر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed report warns that when the community walks in al-muṭayṭāʾ and Persians and Romans serve them, their strife will be among themselves; the term means swaggering with arms extended.
rows.anchor: والمطيطاء: التبختر ومد اليدين في المشي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated phrase is successive threat and warning, four warnings corresponding to four faults in Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: تهديد بعد تهديد، ووعيد بعد وعيد، أي فهو وعيد أربعة لأربعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The four faults are failure to believe the Messenger, failure to pray before God, denial, and turning away from prayer; strutting predated denial.
rows.anchor: فترك التصديق خصلة، والتكذيب خصلة، وترك الصلاة خصلة، والتولي عن الله تعالى خصلة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada explains that swaggering home was the man’s prior habit, so it is not a fifth fault.
rows.anchor: فإنا نقول: تلك كانت عادته قبل التكذيب والتولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One occasion report says the Prophet met Abu Jahl by the Banu Makhzum gate, took and shook his hand, and threatened him; Abu Jahl boasted of his status, and the words were revealed as spoken.
rows.anchor: فاستقبله أبو جهل على باب المسجد، مما يلي باب بني مخزوم، فأخذ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi calls awlā a word of threat and cites a poem repeating it.
rows.anchor: وهي كلمة وعيد. قال الشاعر: فأولى ثم أولى ثم أولى

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada reports Abu Jahl swaggering as the Prophet took his hand and warned him; Abu Jahl said neither the Prophet nor his Lord could harm him, but he was killed miserably at Badr.
rows.anchor: أبو جهل بن هشام يتبختر، فأخذ النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بيده

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view glosses awlā as woe to you, supported by al-Khansāʾ’s poem.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه: الويل لك ومنه قول الخنساء: هممت بنفسي كل الهموم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: On the woe view, it means woe in life, at death, resurrection and Hell; Qurtubi calls this weak.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: الويل لك حيا، والويل لك ميتا، والويل لك يوم البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi rejects as weak the interpretation that awlā means woe repeated through life, death, resurrection and Hell.
rows.anchor: وهذا التكرير كما قال: لك الويلات إنك مرجلي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the phrase to mean condemnation is more fitting than withholding it, with a completion omitted because the expression is frequent.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه الذم لك أولى من تركه، إلا أنه كثير في الكلام فحذف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says the addressee is more deserving and suited to punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى أنت أولى وأجدر بهذا العذاب

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi says awlā means approaching destruction, from the root for nearness.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي: «أولى» في كلام العرب معناه مقاربة الهلاك

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Asmaʿi cites poems using awlā for something that has nearly come or is near to afflicting a person.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الأصمعي: وأولى أن يكون له الولاء

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab praises al-Asmaʿi’s explanation as unmatched.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو العباس ثعلب يستحسن قول الأصمعي

rows.speaker: النحاس
rows.claim: Al-Nahhas glosses awlā laka as nearly perishing then escaping, with destruction closer or more fitting.
rows.anchor: النحاس: العرب تقول أولى لك: كدت تهلك ثم أفلت

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says awlā is not a comparative but predicates an omitted subject; Abu Zayd’s feminine form shows it is not an elative.
rows.anchor: المهدوي قال: ولا تكون أولى أفعل منك، وتكون خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this analysis, laka is the predicate; awlā is indeclinable because it became a proper name for a threat, like Aḥmad.
rows.anchor: فدخول علامة التأنيث دليل على أنه ليس كذلك. و«لك» خبر عن «أولى».

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation distributes the repeated threat across the first, second, third and fourth bad deeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: التكرير فيه على معنى ألزم لك على عملك السيىء الأول

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and Mujahid say the son of Adam is not left neglected without commands or prohibitions; camels left grazing without a herder illustrate sudā.
rows.anchor: أي أن يخلى مهملا، فلا يؤمر ولا ينهى قاله ابن زيد ومجاهد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view asks whether a person is left in the grave forever without resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أيحسب أن يترك في قبره كذلك أبدا لا يبعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem says God left nothing neglected, illustrating sudā.
rows.anchor: وقال الشاعر: فأقسم بالله جهد اليمين ما ترك الله شيئا سدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nutfa is a drop of semen poured into the womb; manā is linked to spilling blood, and nutfa denotes a little water.
rows.anchor: أي من قطرة ماء تمنى في الرحم، أي تراق فيه ولذلك سميت منى لإراقة الدماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nutfa is a small amount of water; natafa means drip, and the drop comes from the man’s loins and woman’s ribs.
rows.anchor: والنطفة: الماء القليل يقال: نطف الماء: إذا قطر

rows.speaker: حفص
rows.claim: Hafs, Ibn Muhaysin, Mujahid, Yaʿqub and ʿAyyash from Abu ʿAmr read with yāʾ to match manī; Abu ʿUbayd selects it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حفص «من مني يمنى» بالياء، وهي قراءة ابن محيصن ومجاهد ويعقوب وعياش عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Other readers use tāʾ to match nutfa, which Abu Hatim selects.
rows.anchor: الباقون بالتاء لأجل النطفة. واختاره أبو حاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿalaqa is blood after the nutfa; the sequence shows God’s ordering from a lowly origin.
rows.anchor: أي دما بعد النطفة، أي قد رتبه تعالى بهذا كله على خسة قدره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-khalaqa means determined; fa-sawwā means fashioned and proportioned, placing the spirit within.
rows.anchor: أي فسواه تسوية، وعدله تعديلا، يجعل الروح فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Minhu can refer to the human or, in another view, semen; the pair is male and female.
rows.anchor: أي من الإنسان. وقيل: من المني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some used the male-female pair to argue for setting aside the intersex case; Qurtubi says the verse speaks of the usual pattern and points to earlier legal discussions.
rows.anchor: وقد احتج بهذا من رأى إسقاط الخنثى

words: أَلَيْسَ ذَٰلِكَ بِقَٰدِرٍ عَلَىٰٓ أَن يُحْيِۦَ ٱلْمَوْتَىٰ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who created a person from a drop can restore the dead bodily after decay.
rows.anchor: أي أليس الذي قدر على خلق هذه النسمة من قطرة من ماء

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is reported to say Subḥānaka Allāhumma balā when reciting this verse.
rows.anchor: وروي عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: أنه كان إذا قرأها قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says to respond to al-Aʿlā with Subḥāna rabbī al-aʿlā and to the end of this sūra with Subḥānaka Allāhumma balā, whether leading prayer or not.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: من قرأ سبح اسم ربك الأعلى

words: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَنزِيلًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is truly sent down by God; the Prophet did not invent it or produce it on his own, despite the polytheists’ claim.
rows.anchor: ما افتريته ولا جئت به من عندك، ولا من تلقاء نفسك

words: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا عَلَيْكَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ تَنزِيلًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the prior promises and threats, the verse establishes that the book contains what people need and is truth, not magic, soothsaying or poetry.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر أصناف الوعد والوعيد، بين أن هذا الكتاب يتضمن ما بالناس حاجة إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Qur’an came in portions, verse after verse, not all at once, explaining nazalnā.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أنزل القرآن متفرقا: آية بعد آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi glosses patience with God’s decree.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى: { فاصبر لحكم ربك } أي لقضاء ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s view: endure polytheist abuse as decreed; this was later abrogated by the fighting verse.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: اصبر على أذى المشركين هكذا قضيت

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says to be patient in the acts of obedience God imposed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي اصبر لما حكم به عليك من الطاعات

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further view says to await God’s promised victory without haste, since it will certainly come.
rows.anchor: أو انتظر حكم الله إذا وعدك أنه ينصرك عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Athim means a sinner and kafūr an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: آثما } أي ذا إثم { أو كفورا } أي لا تطع الكفار

words: وَلَا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِمًا أَوْ كَفُورًا
rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Maʿmar transmits Qatada’s report that Abu Jahl threatened to trample Muhammad’s neck if he saw him praying; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة قال: قال أبو جهل: إن رأيت محمدا يصلي لأطأن على عنقه

words: وَلَا تُطِعْ مِنْهُمْ آثِمًا أَوْ كَفُورًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another occasion account concerns ʿUtba and al-Walid, who offered wealth and marriage in exchange for abandoning prophethood.
rows.anchor: نزلت في عتبة بن ربيعة والوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil specifies that ʿUtba offered his daughter without dowry if Muhammad withdrew, while al-Walid promised money if wealth was his motive.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: الذي عرض التزويج عتبة بن ربيعة قال: إن بناتي من أجمل نساء قريش

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says aw is more emphatic than waw because each of the sinner and unbeliever is individually someone not to obey.
rows.anchor: قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Māʾ mahīn is a weak, lowly substance, namely the semen drop.
rows.anchor: أي ضعيف حقير وهو النطفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says this verse is used as proof by those who hold that the embryo comes from the man’s fluid alone.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية أصل لمن قال: إن خلق الجنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The secure place is the womb.
rows.anchor: أي في مكان حريز وهو الرحم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the term lasts until the embryo is formed.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: إلى أن نصوره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation takes the known term as the time of birth.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إلى وقت الولادة

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafiʿ and al-Kisaʾi double the dāl; others lighten it, and authorities say both forms can mean the same.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع والكسائي «فقدرنا» بالتشديد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A Prophetic report about the crescent says that when it is obscured one should estimate its course and stations.
rows.anchor: قول النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في الهلال: «إذا غم عليكم فاقدروا له»

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says light and doubled forms can share a meaning, citing readings of the phrase about apportioning death.
rows.anchor: قال محمد ابن الجهم عن الفراء: «فقدرنا» قال:

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says Arabic combines parallel forms, citing the two imperatives in 86:17 and a poem by al-Aʿshā.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: وتجمع العرب بين اللغتين قال الله تعالى: فمهل الكافرين أمهلهم رويدا

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima reads lightly from the sense of power; Abu ʿUbayd, Abu Hatim and al-Kisaʾi select it because the verse later says al-qādirūn.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عكرمة { فقدرنا } مخففة من القدرة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: The doubled reading means determining the wretched and happy; Qurtubi attributes this to a report from the Prophet through Ibn Masʿud.
rows.anchor: رواه ابن مسعود عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says God determined shortness or tallness.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى قدرنا قصيرا أو طويلا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas explains qadarnā as exercising mastery or control.
rows.anchor: ونحوه عن ابن عباس: قدرنا ملكنا

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says this fits the light reading; Qurtubi agrees, noting that ʿIkrima reads it lightly as we exercised mastery.
rows.anchor: المهدوي: وهذا التفسير أشبه بقراءة التخفيف. قلت:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi lists the doubled reading’s senses: setting birth and developmental stages, determining felicity or misery, or determining height; some say both readings mean the same.
rows.anchor: فأفادت الكلمتان معنيين متغايرين أي قدرنا وقت الولادة وأحوال النطفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marṣād is mifaʿāl from raṣad, something lying ahead.
rows.anchor: مفعال من الرصد والرصد: كل شيء كان أمامك

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan describes a checkpoint at Hell: none reaches Paradise without crossing; a person with a pass crosses and one without it is detained.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: إن على النار رصدا، لا يدخل أحد الجنة

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: Sufyan says there are three bridges over Hell.
rows.anchor: وعن سفيان رضي الله عنه قال: عليها ثلاث قناطر

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parsing makes marṣād mean possessing watchers who watch passersby.
rows.anchor: وقيل «مرصادا» ذات أرصاد على النسب، أي ترصد من يمر بها

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil glosses marṣād as a prison.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: محبسا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view calls it a road or passage, so reaching Paradise requires crossing Hell.
rows.anchor: وقيل: طريقا وممرا، فلا سبيل إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: الصحاح
rows.claim: Al-Ṣiḥāḥ records that marṣād means a road.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: والمرصاد: الطريق

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri defines a marṣād as a place for watching an enemy, like a place for training horses; angels watch unbelievers until they descend to Hell.
rows.anchor: وذكر القشيري: أن المرصاد المكان الذي يرصد فيه الواحد العدو

rows.speaker: أبو سنان
rows.claim: Al-Mawardi cites Abu Sinan: marṣād means a watcher who repays people according to their deeds.
rows.anchor: عن أبي سنان أنها بمعنى راصدة، تجازيهم بأفعالهم

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿi and al-Kisaʾi distinguish watching from preparing something; tarassud is waiting and marṣad is a watch post.
rows.anchor: الأصمعي: رصدته أرصده: ترقبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi concludes Hell is prepared and waiting for those who come to it.
rows.anchor: قلت: فجهنم معدة مترصدة، متفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mifaʿāl is an intensive pattern, suggesting Hell’s frequent waiting for unbelievers.
rows.anchor: والمرصاد مفعال من أبنية المبالغة كالمعطار والمغيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lit-tāghīn maʾāb is an appositive to marṣād; maʾāb means return, from āba yaʾūbu.
rows.anchor: بدل من قوله: «مرصادا» والمآب: المرجع

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses maʾāb as a refuge or dwelling.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: مأوى ومنزلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transgressors are those who transgress in religion through unbelief or in worldly life through oppression.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالطاغين من طغى في دينه بالكفر، أو في دنياه بالظلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their stay lasts through endless successive epochs, one following another.
rows.anchor: أي ماكثين في النار ما دامت الأحقاب، وهي لا تنقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥuqb means an age, ḥuqba a year; ḥuqub is said to be eighty years, more or less.
rows.anchor: والحقب بضمتين: الدهر والأحقاب الدهور

rows.speaker: متمم بن نويرة
rows.claim: Tamim ibn Nuwayra uses ḥuqba for a period of time in a cited poem.
rows.anchor: قال متمم بن نويرة التميمي: وكنا كندماني جذيمة حقبة من الدهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi takes the epochs as unending epochs of the hereafter, omitted by context; five or ten specified epochs would imply a limit.
rows.anchor: والمعنى في الآية لابثين فيها أحقاب الآخرة التي لا نهاية لها فحذف الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabs named the longest duration they imagined as a figure for perpetuity, a euphemism for remaining forever.
rows.anchor: وذكر الأحقاب لأن الحقب كان أبعد شيء عندهم، فتكلم بما تذهب إليه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says epochs rather than days sound more dreadful and indicate lasting punishment.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ذكر الأحقاب دون الأيام لأن الأحقاب أهول في القلوب، وأدل على الخلود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says these meanings are close and this endless duration concerns unbelievers.
rows.anchor: والمعنى متقارب وهذا الخلود في حق المشركين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse could instead concern sinners who leave the Fire after epochs.
rows.anchor: ويمكن حمل الآية على العصاة الذين يخرجون من النار بعد أحقاب

words: لَا يَذُوقُونَ فِيهَا بَرْدًۭا وَلَا شَرَابًا
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes the epochs the time of drinking boiling water and ghassaq; afterward another punishment begins.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الأحقاب وقت لشربهم الحميم والغساق، فءذا انقضت فيكون لهم نوع آخر من العقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Moses story consoles Muhammad: Pharaoh was stronger than contemporary unbelievers, yet God seized him and will do likewise to them.
rows.anchor: وهذا تسلية للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم. أي إن فرعون كان أقوى من كفار عصرك

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes hal as mā: the Prophet was told an account that had not come to him before, as a lesson for the fearful.
rows.anchor: وقيل: «هل» بمعنى «ما» أي ما أتاك، ولكن أخبرت به

rows.speaker: ابن محيصن
rows.claim: Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn ʿAmir and Kufans read Ṭuwā with tanwin; Abu ʿUbayd selects the lighter proper-name form.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن محيصن وابن عامر والكوفيون «طوى» منونا واختاره أبو عبيد لخفة الاسم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Other readers omit tanwin, treating it as a diptote; al-Farraʾ says it is a valley between Medina and Egypt, shifted from Ṭāwin.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: طوى: واد بين المدينة ومصر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and ʿIkrima, and a report from Abu ʿAmr, read kasra for “sanctified repeatedly”; al-Zajjaj adduces a poem.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وعكرمة «طوى» بكسر الطاء، وروي عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view treats the u- and i-vowels as dialect variants; Qurtubi refers to earlier discussion in Ṭā Hā.
rows.anchor: وقيل: ضم الطاء وكسرها لغتان، وقد مضى في «طه» القول فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The call from God is omitted because a call is speech, and the text proceeds directly to the command to go.
rows.anchor: أي ناداه ربه، فحذف، لأن النداء قول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh exceeded the bounds in disobedience.
rows.anchor: أي جاوز القدر في العصيان

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Pharaoh was a non-Arab from Hamadan.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الحسن قال: كان فرعون علجا من همدان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Pharaoh came from Istakhr.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد قال: كان من أهل إصطخر

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Another al-Hasan report places Pharaoh in Isfahan, names him Dhū Ẓufr and says he was four handspans tall.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن أيضا قال: من أهل أصبهان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invitation is to become Muslim and be purified of sins.
rows.anchor: أي تسلم فتطهر من الذنوب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s interpretation as a call to testify that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس قال: هل لك أن تشهد أن لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses offers guidance to obey the Lord, so Pharaoh will fear and heed Him.
rows.anchor: أي وأرشدك إلى طاعة ربك

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafiʿ and Ibn Kathir double zāy by assimilating the original tāʾ of tatazakkā.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وابن كثير «تزكى» بتشديد الزاي، على إدغام التاء في الزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other readers use a light zāy, with the tāʾ dropped.
rows.anchor: الباقون: «تزكى» بتخفيف الزاي على معنى طرح التاء

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr says the doubled form means give charity and the light form become a pure believer; he selects the latter as Moses invited Pharaoh to belief.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو: «تزكى» بالتشديد تتصدق ب الصدقة

rows.speaker: صخر بن جويرية
rows.claim: Sakhr ibn Juwayriyya reports Moses asking how to approach Pharaoh when he knew he would refuse; God ordered him to go and said twelve thousand angels seek knowledge of the decree without attaining it.
rows.anchor: قال صخر بن جويرية: لما بعث الله موسى إلى فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The great sign means the supreme miracle.
rows.anchor: أي العلامة العظمى وهي المعجزة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some identify the sign as the staff, others the bright hand shining like the sun.
rows.anchor: وقيل: العصا. وقيل: اليد البيضاء تبرق كالشمس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak transmits Ibn Abbas’s view that it was the staff; al-Hasan says hand and staff.
rows.anchor: وروى الضحاك عن ابن عباس: الآية الكبرى قال العصا. الحسن: يده وعصاه

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other views identify the sign as the splitting of the sea or all of Moses’ signs and miracles.
rows.anchor: وقيل: فلق البحر. وقيل: الآية: إشارة إلى جميع آياته ومعجزاته

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi rejects identifying the man addressed as al-Walid, Umayya or al-ʿAbbas: Ibn Umm Maktum was in Medina while Walid and Umayya were in Mecca and could not meet; they died unbelievers, and Umayya never came to Medina.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: أما قول علمائنا إنه الوليد بن المغيرة فقد قال آخرون إنه أمية بن خلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Umm Maktum came while the Prophet addressed Quraysh leaders, hoping for their conversion and their clans’ conversion; the blind man repeatedly asked to be taught, unaware the Prophet was occupied.
rows.anchor: أقبل ابن أم مكتوم والنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم مشتغل بمن حضره من وجوه قريش يدعوهم إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As Ibn Umm Maktum persisted, displeasure appeared on the Prophet’s face; he feared the leaders would call his followers blind, lowly and enslaved, then frowned and turned away, prompting revelation.
rows.anchor: حتى ظهرت الكراهة في وجه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لقطعة كلامه

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawri says afterward the Prophet spread his cloak for Ibn Umm Maktum, welcomed the man reproached on his account, and asked about his need.
rows.anchor: قال الثوري: " فكان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بعد ذلك إذا رأى ابن أم مكتوم

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawri adds that the Prophet appointed Ibn Umm Maktum governor of Medina twice during two campaigns.
rows.anchor: واستخلفه على المدينة مرتين في غزوتين غزاهما

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: Anas says he saw Ibn Umm Maktum at al-Qadisiyya mounted in armor with a black banner.
rows.anchor: قال أنس: فرأيته يوم القادسية راكبا وعليه درع ومعه راية سوداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars say the interruption would be poor manners only if Ibn Umm Maktum knew the Prophet was occupied and hoped to win the leaders’ faith.
rows.anchor: قال علماؤنا: ما فعله ابن أم مكتوم كان من سوء الأدب لو كان عالما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God reproached the Prophet either to protect the people of the bench from hurt or to teach that a poor believer is better than a rich one.
rows.anchor: ولكن الله تبارك وتعالى عاتبه حتى لا تنكسر قلوب أهل الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attending to a poor believer was better, although turning to the rich in hope of conversion also served a purpose.
rows.anchor: وكان النظر إلى المؤمن أولى وإن كان فقيرا أصلح وأولى من الأمر الآخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi applies the same priority principle to the verse about a prophet not taking captives, as discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا يخرج قوله تعالى: ما كان لنبي أن يكون له أسرى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says the Prophet sought to conciliate the Quraysh leader, confident Ibn Umm Maktum already had faith.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنما قصد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم تأليف الرجل، ثقة بما كان في قلب ابن أم مكتوم
